title: Permissions in a member community
metaTitle: Show what a member is allowed to do
excerpt: Show a member what they can do in the community, and why an action is unavailable. A hidden reply box feels like a bug. A disabled one with a reason feels like a rule.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table, a room where it is obvious who may speak.
caption: In a room, people can see who has the floor. The product should be that clear. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a community hide buttons a member cannot use?
faqs.answer: Hide tools a member should never think about, such as moderator queues and billing, and do not hide actions they reasonably expect, such as reply or post. If they expect the action, show it unavailable and say why. A missing reply box looks broken, while a disabled one with a sentence looks like a rule.

faqs.question: When should the reason appear?
faqs.answer: Show the reason before they write, not after they tap Post. If a room is read-only until they say hello in Welcome, the composer should say that on arrival. Letting them draft a long post and then rejecting it teaches them that the product wastes their time. The rule belongs where the action is.

faqs.question: What should a member see in a room they can read but not post in?
faqs.answer: They should see the posts, and a plain line where the composer would be that names the rule, such as announcements only or an intro required before replies. Lurking is a legitimate state. Pretending the composer fell off the page is not.

markdown:
Member community permissions UX is the difference between a rule and a bug. Show a person what they can do, and why something they expected is unavailable. A hidden reply box feels broken. A visible one with a reason feels like the room has a host.

The person in question is still deciding whether to post or lurk. Permissions are part of that decision. If they can read and not speak, say so before they spend ten minutes on a draft. If they can speak in one room and not another, the rooms should look different for a reason you wrote down, not because a button vanished.

## What they are allowed to do, in one glance

A member should be able to answer three questions without opening a help doc. Can I read this? Can I reply? If I cannot reply, why not?

Put the answers on the object. A thread that is open for replies has a composer. A thread that is closed has a line where the composer was: "Replies are closed. A host can still post updates." An announcements room has the same line at the top of the composer area, every time, not only after a failed attempt.

Do not make them infer the rule from absence. Absence is how software looks when it failed to load. People who are already nervous about posting will blame themselves, then blame you, then go quiet. The quiet will look like low engagement in your dashboard. It was a missing sentence.

Write the allowed actions as verbs they already use. Read. Reply. React. Start a thread. Invite. Edit your own reply. Report. If a verb is not allowed, it still gets a sentence when it is a verb they would look for. Invite and edit are verbs they look for. "Purge cache" is not. Hide the ones that belong to staff.

The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines exist so people can perceive content, operate the interface, and understand it. A control that is not in the accessibility tree because it was hidden, and a control that is visible but unexplained, both fail the person who is trying to operate the room. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is worth reading before you decide that "they'll figure it out" is a permission model. Understanding is part of the standard, not a nice extra.

## Hidden, disabled, or explained

Use three treatments, and pick them on purpose.

Hide an action when the member should not know it exists. Moderator tools, other members' private notes, billing for a community they do not pay for, and staff-only deletes belong in this group. Showing a disabled "Ban member" to a new arrival is a different product leaking into theirs.

Disable an action when they know it exists and today they cannot use it. Reply in a read-only room. Post before the required intro. Edit after the edit window has closed. The control stays where they expect it, it does not look tappable, and a sentence says what would make it available.

Explain without a control when the action is not theirs at all and a disabled button would tease them. "Only hosts post in Announcements." That sentence replaces the composer. There is nothing to tap. There is also nothing to hunt for.

The failure mode is the fourth treatment, which teams ship by accident: the button is gone, the layout collapses, and no sentence appears. Designers call it clean. Members call it broken. Clean is not the goal. Predictable is the goal.

If the reason is temporary, say the condition, not a vague later. "You can reply after you post a short intro in Welcome." Include the way to do that condition. A reason with no path is a wall. A reason with a path is a rule they can finish.

## Rules a member actually runs into

Read but not post. This is the common case for a new account, a lurker role, or a room that is a bulletin. Show the posts in full. Put the reason in the composer slot. Do not blur the posts to force an upgrade unless the business really sells access that way, and if it does, say what paying changes. Blur without a price or a rule looks like a glitch.

Post in some rooms only. The room list should mark the ones they can speak in, in text, not only with a color dot. "You can reply" next to a room name is enough. When they open a room they cannot speak in, repeat the reason. Do not rely on them remembering a legend from settings.

Edit or delete their own post. If there is a window, say it at the moment of posting and again if they come back too late. "You can edit this for a short time" is weaker than "You can edit this until someone replies" or whatever rule you actually chose. Pick a rule you can explain in one line. If you cannot explain it, the rule is too clever for the room.

Mentions and direct messages. If a member cannot be messaged, the message action on their profile should say so. "Ada is not taking messages" is a complete design. A missing icon makes the sender think the profile failed to load.

Invites. If only hosts can invite, the invite control on a member's account should not be a haunted menu they find by long-pressing. Either it is absent for a reason you do not need to advertise, or, if they will look for it because someone told them to invite a colleague, it is present and disabled with "Hosts send invites."

Staff viewing as a member. Build a real member preview. An admin who "sees what members see" while still holding admin rights will approve a screen no member has. The preview account should fail the same actions a new member fails, and it should show the same sentences.

## Write the reason before they compose

The expensive mistake is letting someone write and then telling them they were not allowed. You have spent their attention and their nerve. Recovery is poor. They rarely rewrite the post in the correct room.

Put the block on the way in. If Welcome is required, the other rooms can show their threads, and the composer slot points at Welcome. If a thread is locked, the composer is already replaced when they land. If their account is limited after a report, say the limit in human language at the top of any composer that remains. "A host has limited your posting today" is stark and clear. A failing submit with a 403 is how you turn a moderation decision into a support ticket.

Do not use shame as the interface. The reason can be firm without a lecture. They do not need a paragraph about community values at the moment of a disabled button. One line. A link if the policy is long. The policy page is not the permission. The line on the object is the permission.

Keep the reason stable. If the button's tooltip says one thing and the error after tap says another, you have two policies. Pick the stricter one, show it first, and delete the other string from the product.

## What lurkers need the interface to admit

Lurking is a valid use of a community. A person who reads for a month and then posts once is not a broken funnel. Permissions should make lurking comfortable and posting legible.

Comfortable lurking means they can tell they are not behind. Do not show them a disabled Post covered in warning color on every screen as if silence were a fault. A quiet line is enough.

Legible posting means that when they are ready, the step is obvious and the audience is obvious. "This reply will notify people in the thread, not the whole community" belongs next to the button if that is true. Fear of notifying everyone is one of the main reasons people do not post. If your product does notify everyone, say that too. Surprise notifications are how a first post becomes a last post.

Reactions are a useful middle. If they cannot post yet but they can react, show the reaction control and say they can reply after the intro. A small allowed action teaches the permission model faster than a document does.

## Review it like a member who expected a button

Make a list of every action a reasonable member will look for in the first session. For each one, mark hide, disable with reason, or show. Then build those states. A permission matrix in a spreadsheet that never reaches the screen is a private note, not a design.

On a phone, as a new member, open a room you cannot post in. The test passes if you can read the reason without tapping, and if you never meet a spinner where the composer should be. Spinners that end in emptiness are indistinguishable from bugs.

Search is the next place this shows up. People who cannot see why a room is closed start hunting for the thread someone mentioned. The next piece is [search inside a member community](/blog/search-inside-a-member-community). It should return the room in their words and still tell them, on the result, whether they can speak there.

If you want the rules of a product written into the interface instead of into a follow-up email, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). A permission nobody can see is not a permission. It is a support queue.
